title: Organic Startup Ideas: build what you wish someone would make for you
summary: Paul Graham argues the best startup ideas grow organically from your own life rather than being decided from afar. Focus on fixing things that seem broken, don't worry about whether it's a company, and don't be put off if others call it a toy.

principles.text: Find ideas by asking what you wish someone would make for you.
principles.quote: The best way to come up with startup ideas is to ask yourself the question: what do you wish someone would make for you?

principles.text: Organic ideas, born from your own needs, beat made-up ideas for others; the most successful startups skew organic.
principles.quote: There is no sharp line between the two types of ideas, but the most successful startups seem to be closer to the Apple type than the Viaweb type.

principles.text: Young founders especially should avoid made-up ideas, since predicting what others want takes experience.
principles.quote: It takes experience to predict what other people will want. The worst ideas we see at Y Combinator are from young founders making things they think other people will want.

principles.text: Focus on the idea, not the startup: fix broken things without asking if it's company-sized.
principles.quote: I'd encourage you to focus more on the idea part and less on the startup part. Just fix things that seem broken, regardless of whether it seems like the problem is important enough to build a company on.

principles.text: Being dismissed as a toy is a good sign; it explains why others overlooked the idea.
principles.quote: Don't be discouraged if what you produce initially is something other people dismiss as a toy. In fact, that's a good sign.

principles.text: The most valuable opportunity is an unmet need that is just becoming fixable; use the latest tech to spot it first.
principles.quote: There's nothing more valuable than an unmet need that is just becoming fixable.
